content: School tobacco policies (STPs) are considered a potentially effective method to prevent smoking initiation among adolescents, as the school environment can significantly influence young people's smoking behaviors. These policies are cost-effective, relatively simple to implement, and can reach a large population. However, their actual effectiveness in preventing smoking uptake remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of school-based policies aimed at preventing smoking initiation among students by regulating smoking within the school environment. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across seven electronic bibliographic databases, including the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group specialized register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and ERIC. Additional searches were performed in grey literature and ongoing trial resources, with the most recent search completed in May 2014. The review included cluster-randomized controlled trials (c-RCTs) where primary and secondary schools were randomized to receive varying levels of smoking policy interventions or no intervention at all. Non-randomized controlled trials, interrupted time series, and controlled before-and-after studies were also considered eligible. Cross-sectional studies were not formally included in the review but were described to generate hypotheses for future research. The data collection and analysis process involved independent assessment of studies for inclusion. Due to the limited quality of the available studies, a formal meta-analysis could not be conducted, and the findings were synthesized narratively. Only one study met the inclusion criteria for this review. This study, conducted in two middle schools in different regions of China, was judged to have a high risk of bias. The intervention school implemented a tobacco policy, environmental changes, and communication activities, while the control school received no intervention. After one year of follow-up, there was no observed difference in smoking prevalence between the intervention and control schools. Additionally, 24 observational studies were described to generate hypotheses. In these studies, policy exposure was primarily assessed through face-to-face interviews with school staff, and outcomes were evaluated using self-administered questionnaires. Most of these studies reported no significant differences in smoking prevalence between schools with formal STPs and those without such policies. Even in schools with highly enforced policies—where smoking bans extended to outdoor spaces, involved teachers, included sanctions for violations, provided assistance for smokers to quit, and were supported by prevention programs—there was no significant reduction in smoking prevalence compared to schools with weaker or no policies. The authors concluded that, despite an extensive literature search and rigorous evaluation of studies, there is no reliable evidence to support the effectiveness of STPs in preventing smoking initiation among students. This lack of evidence is concerning from a public health perspective. To address this gap, well-designed randomized controlled trials or quasi-experimental studies are urgently needed to evaluate the effectiveness of school tobacco policies.
